chapters.title: Chapter 3: Pulling the Three Working Capital Levers

lessons.title: Managing Receivables: Credit Terms, Collections and TReDS

children.text: Receivables are the lever most businesses pull last and should pull first. Inventory takes months to fix and supplier terms need negotiation, but the money customers already owe you is sitting there, earned, invoiced and legally yours. Konkan Ceramics has ₹2.4 crore of it. This lesson is about deciding who gets credit, collecting what is owed, and using the Indian machinery built specifically to get suppliers paid faster.

body.text: Giving credit is lending money. A business that would never approve a ₹20 lakh loan will hand a new dealer ₹20 lakh of goods on 60-day terms after one good meeting.

children.text: Credit Is a Decision, Not a Default

In most Indian SMEs, credit terms are set by whoever closes the deal, under pressure, at the end of a negotiation. A credit policy replaces that with three decisions made in advance, in the cold light of day.
Who gets credit at all.
New customers can start on advance payment or part payment, and earn terms over two or three clean cycles.
How much.
Every customer needs a credit limit, a maximum outstanding beyond which supply stops until they pay.
For how long.
The credit period, written into the order, not implied by habit.
The evaluation itself does not need a credit department. For an Indian business buyer, a competent check takes about thirty minutes.

body.title: Thirty-minute credit check on a new buyer
steps: Verify the GSTIN on the GST portal and check whether the buyer files returns on time. A buyer months behind on GST filings is usually months behind on payments too.
If it is a company, pull the MCA master data and the latest filed financials for turnover, net worth and charges registered against its assets.
Obtain a commercial credit report, such as CIBIL Rank or a CRIF report, for its borrowing and default history.
Ask for two trade references from suppliers in your own industry, and actually call them.
Search for the name along with words such as winding up, NCLT and cheque bounce.
Visit the premises or the godown once, in person, if the limit is meaningful.
Start small. Set a first limit you could write off without losing sleep, and raise it only after two or three clean cycles.

body.text: Security is worth asking for and worth understanding. A post-dated cheque gives you recourse under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 if it bounces, but recovering money through that route takes years. A bank guarantee, a letter of credit or a security deposit are far stronger, and a personal guarantee from the promoter changes behaviour more than any of them.

children.text: The Ageing Report Is the Whole Game
A single receivables total tells you nothing. Split it by how overdue it is, and the problems announce themselves. Here is Konkan Ceramics, which sells on 60-day terms.

cells: Healthy. This is the cost of doing business on credit
Usually process friction: wrong invoice details, missing paperwork, a payment run missed
Now a pattern. These customers are managing their cash using yours
Serious. Supply should already have stopped
Assume this is a recovery problem, not a collection problem
Half of all receivables are past due

body.title: Konkan Ceramics: receivables by ageing bucket (₹ lakh)

stats.label: Overdue
stats.context: Half the receivables book, already earned

stats.label: Cost of a ₹10 lakh write-off
stats.context: At a 10% net margin, that is what it takes to replace it

body.text: Read that last stat to your sales team. Writing off ₹10 lakh does not cost ₹10 lakh, it costs the entire profit on ₹1 crore of sales. The effort of collecting one stuck invoice is almost always cheaper than the effort of replacing it.

body.title: Where does Monday morning go?
body.question: You have one collections executive and four problem accounts: A owes ₹40 lakh, 20 days overdue, always pays eventually. B owes ₹18 lakh, 75 days overdue, has stopped taking calls. C owes ₹3 lakh, 100 days overdue, business has shut. D owes ₹22 lakh, not yet due, but the due date is Friday. Where should the effort go first?
options: C, because it is the oldest and most overdue
A, because it is the largest amount outstanding
B first, then a call on D before Friday, because B is still recoverable and D can be prevented from going overdue at all
Split the day evenly across all four so nobody is ignored
body.explanation: B is large, deteriorating and still collectable, so it has the highest value at risk. D costs one phone call and stops a fresh overdue from being created, which is the cheapest collection there is. A is annoying but behaving to a known pattern. C is a recovery and provisioning matter for the finance team and a lawyer, not a use of your collector's Monday.

children.text: Collections Is a Process, Not a Personality
Good collections are boring and scheduled. The single highest-return change most Indian businesses can make is to stop calling after the due date and start calling before it.

cells: Invoice sent with the correct GSTIN, PO number and delivery proof attached
Polite confirmation call: is the invoice approved and in the payment run?
Payment expected. Any dispute should already be known by now
Written reminder with a statement of account attached
Escalation to the buyer's finance head, copying your sales manager
Supply hold on further orders, communicated in writing
Formal demand letter, and for an MSME seller, the option of the Samadhaan route

body.text: Most overdue invoices in India are not refusals to pay, they are paperwork. A wrong GSTIN, a missing purchase order number, an unsigned delivery challan or an invoice sent to a person who left. Fixing invoice accuracy usually clears the 1 to 30 day bucket faster than any amount of chasing.

body.title: What an early payment discount really costs

children.text: Offering 2% off for payment 30 days early feels like a small concession. Annualise it.

content.caption: The price of buying your own money back early

children.text: 2% for 30 days:
about 24.8% a year.
1% for 15 days:
about 24.6% a year.
Your cash credit limit:
around 11% a year.

So a routine 2% discount is roughly twice the cost of borrowing from your bank. That does not make it wrong. It makes it a financing decision that should be priced, capped, offered selectively to slow payers, and withdrawn once collections improve, rather than left standing in every price list forever.

body.title: Price the discount
body.prompt: A customer offers to pay 30 days earlier than the agreed terms if you give a 2% discount. Using the formula above, what is the annualised cost of that discount, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: 2 divided by 98 is 0.0204, and 365 divided by 30 is 12.17. Multiply them and you get about 24.8% a year. You are effectively borrowing your own money at 24.8% from a customer who already owes it to you. Compare that with a cash credit limit at around 11% before agreeing.

children.text: The Indian Machinery for Getting Paid
India has built specific infrastructure for this problem, largely because delayed payment to small suppliers is so widespread. If you sell to large buyers, these are the tools that matter.

body.caption: Ways to turn an invoice into cash before its due date

cells: Invoice is uploaded to an RBI-authorised exchange, the buyer accepts it, and financiers bid to pay you now at a discount
MSME sellers supplying large corporates or PSUs
Your bank advances against accepted invoices, usually with recourse to you if the buyer defaults
A factor buys the receivable outright, and may take on the credit risk
Businesses wanting the risk off their books
You pay the customer, in effect, for paying sooner
Borrow against the whole receivables and stock pool
General working capital, covered in Chapter 5

body.title: How a TReDS transaction actually runs

events.title: Invoice uploaded
events.description: The MSME supplier uploads the invoice and supporting documents to a platform such as RXIL, M1xchange or Invoicemart.

events.title: Buyer accepts
events.description: The large buyer confirms the invoice on the platform. That acceptance is what makes the receivable financeable at a fine rate.

events.title: Financiers bid
events.description: Banks and NBFCs bid to discount it. Pricing follows the buyer's credit rating, not the supplier's, which is the whole point.

events.title: Supplier is paid
events.description: The winning financier pays the supplier the discounted amount, typically without recourse, so the supplier is out of the credit risk.

events.title: Buyer pays the financier
events.description: The buyer settles on the original due date. The supplier's cash arrived weeks earlier.

body.label: TReDS onboarding is now mandatory for mid-size buyers
body.context: A Ministry of MSME notification dated 7 November 2024 requires all companies with turnover above ₹250 crore, and all Central Public Sector Enterprises, to register on a TReDS platform, with a compliance date of 31 March 2025. The earlier threshold, set in 2018, was ₹500 crore. If you supply a buyer of that size, ask which platform they are on.

body.text: Know your rights as a small supplier. Under Section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006 a buyer must pay within the agreed period, capped at 45 days, or 15 days where there is no written agreement. Under Section 16, delayed payment carries compound interest with monthly rests at three times the RBI bank rate, which is a far heavier rate than ordinary commercial interest. Registering on Udyam and stating your MSME status on every invoice is what puts you in that protection.

body.title: The statutory limit
body.textWithBlank: Under Section 15 of the MSMED Act, 2006, payment to a micro or small supplier cannot exceed ___ days where there is a written agreement.
body.explanation: Forty-five days is the outer limit even if the parties agree to longer, and it is 15 days where there is no written agreement. Buyers who breach it face interest under Section 16 and lose the tax deduction until they actually pay, which Lesson 3.2 covers from the buyer's side.

body.title: The strategic customer who will not pay
body.scenario: Your largest dealer accounts for 22% of Konkan Ceramics' sales and owes ₹48 lakh, of which ₹31 lakh is more than 90 days overdue. He keeps placing orders, pays just enough to keep supply flowing, and reminds your sales head at every meeting that a competitor is courting him. Your bank limit is fully drawn. The sales head insists that stopping supply would be commercial suicide.
body.prompt: How would you handle this, in what order, and what would you be prepared to lose?
body.modelAnswer:
First, see the position clearly.
1. He is not a customer at this point, he is an unsecured lender to us, funded at 11% cash credit, and we are paying the interest.
2. Work out the real profit on his business after that funding cost. At a 10% margin, ₹31 lakh stuck for a year at 11% eats roughly ₹3.4 lakh of profit, which is the entire margin on about ₹34 lakh of sales.
Then act, in this order.
3. Stop the drift. Convert the ₹31 lakh into a written, signed repayment schedule with dates, ideally secured with post-dated cheques or a promoter guarantee.
4. Move new supply to a strict rule: fresh orders only against advance or against payment of one old invoice for each new one, so the exposure cannot grow while the schedule runs.
5. Do not cut him off in one step if 22% of sales genuinely depends on him. Reduce the exposure in stages, and say so plainly and politely at owner level, not through the sales executive.
6. Test the competitor claim. A dealer 90 days overdue with us is usually overdue with others too, and a new supplier will check.
7. Fix the incentive that created this. If sales commissions are paid on billing rather than collection, the sales head is behaving perfectly rationally, and that is the actual problem to solve.
What I am prepared to lose.
8. I would rather lose this dealer than lose another ₹30 lakh. Concentration at 22% is itself the risk, and the plan should include developing two or three alternative dealers in that territory starting now.

cards.definition: The maximum a customer may owe at any time. Supply stops above it until money comes in.
Receivables split by how overdue they are. The single most useful cash document in the business.
An RBI-authorised exchange where MSME invoices accepted by large buyers are financed at the buyer's credit rating.
Borrowing against accepted invoices, usually with recourse if the buyer does not pay.
Selling a receivable outright to a factor, who may also take the credit risk.
Compound interest at three times the RBI bank rate, payable by buyers who pay micro and small suppliers late.

points: Granting credit is lending. Decide who, how much and how long in advance, and check a new buyer before the first consignment leaves.
Manage the ageing report, not the total. Half of Konkan Ceramics' ₹2.4 crore is already overdue.
A ₹10 lakh write-off at a 10% margin needs ₹1 crore of replacement sales. Collecting is always cheaper than reselling.
Call before the due date. Most early overdue amounts are paperwork problems, not payment refusals.
An early payment discount of 2% for 30 days costs about 24.8% a year, roughly twice a cash credit limit. Price it before offering it.
MSME sellers have real machinery: TReDS, now mandatory for buyers above ₹250 crore of turnover, and statutory 45-day payment with compound interest under the MSMED Act.

body.text: Konkan Ceramics is fictional. Statutory provisions are summarised for teaching and can change, and the RBI bank rate varies over time. Confirm the current position with your chartered accountant or legal adviser before relying on it. This is not legal advice.
